utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Where is Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. Mr. Scott was just here with us and he disappeared inexplicably. I can't tell the Trial Chamber where he's gone. I expect that he will -- I think that he must be very close. In fact, he's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise, Mr. President. I was here. I did have to step back out for one moment. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I just want to remind you that you are still under the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sir Martin.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a few more points of background before we move on with your testimony in connection with the structure and operations of ECMM, a couple of additional details which might come up in the Court's review of evidence in the future, so I'll ask you a couple of explanations. In addition to the monitors which made up the various monitoring teams and the various coordinating centres or CCs, such as CC Mostar, did ECMM also have liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had liaison officers in certain UN headquarters. For example, in particular, when we were in Zenica, we had a liaison officer with the UN headquarters in Kiseljak, which was our closest UN headquarters, and he was known as the ECLO, EC liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make pauses between question and answers and speak more slowly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as reflected in Exhibit 86.1, which we were looking at yesterday, finally, in this regard, is it correct that in 1993, the ECMM had a strength of approximately 350 personnel throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. The total strength was about 350, of which some 160 were actually monitors on the ground, and the remainder were headquarters staff, interpreters, drivers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, I want to move forward with your testimony. You told us yesterday that you arrived in the Mostar region at the end of July -- excuse me, at the end of June or early July, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In fact, it was the first few days in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where did you first report to, in terms of just the town or location?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived down in Mostar, we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: They have some difficulties in the French channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll keep trying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, again we are going to both have to make, I think, a further effort to slow down a bit. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Mostar at the beginning of July, 1993, we were not able actually to get into Mostar because the HVO had blocked entry to all international organisations. The CC headquarters, of which I was to be the head, was based in Siroki Brijeg, which was some 15 kilometres to the west of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you spend some time in your first few days or weeks upon arriving in the Siroki Brijeg area trying to gain access to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my fundamental task on arrival. It was intensely frustrating, having been posted to Mostar, not being able to get into Mostar. So almost every day, I was seeking meetings with either the Deputy Defence Minister of the Croats, whose name was Slobodan Bozic, or the Defence Minister Bruno Stojic, arguing constantly for us to get into, first of all, West Mostar, which is the Croat side, and then over into East Mostar, the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, some weeks later, did you, in fact -- I direct your attention first to West Mostar separately from East Mostar for the moment. Did you first obtain access into West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we succeeded in getting into West Mostar after discussions including with Jadranko Prlic, who was the president of the HVO and a political leader. And finally, we got the go-ahead to get into West Mostar, which was sometime I think fairly early August. And then about two weeks later, we managed to get agreement to enter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, Your Honours. On page 4, line 2, apparently, I believe at line 2, the witness said, Yes, we succeeded -- somebody who was the president of the HVO. The record did not pick up that name.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The name is Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Also, apparently, the Minister of Defence's name is not properly in the record either. It's not the witness's fault, I don't believe. We just have many problems some days with translations.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's because of the speed.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try and go a little slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, would you please make clear for us those two names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the name Bruno Stojic is correctly printed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the witness is referring up above --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Slobodan Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're also correct, Witness. At line 21, page 3, Bruno Stojic is also correctly stated. But I agree with counsel that didn't seem to appear the second.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The line above, it's Slobodan Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see. You're correcting --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Briefly, when you arrived in West Mostar for the first time, can you tell the Chamber what you saw, what the condition of that part of Mostar was, what your initial observations were?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was certainly damage in West Mostar, but not nearly as much as I had expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sometime after that -- approximately can you tell us how long after that did you eventually gain access into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about two weeks later that we managed to get into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber briefly whose approval or what steps did you take to get access into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to get -- because the HVO controlled the entrances, it had to be through the Defence Minister and Deputy Defence Minister. In other words, my main link, Slobodan Bozic, to enable us to get through the HVO checkpoints to get round the back of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you share with the Chamber in the next few moments just your initial observations in East Mostar when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: East Mostar was a scene of total, total devastation. I did not see throughout my time there one building that was not damaged by fire. There was constant shelling by the HVO, artillery, mortars, machine-guns, and sniper fire. There were very few people out on the streets. And as soon as the first shell landed, the streets would empty completely. And people would dive to try to get down into cellars. There was no water and no electricity in East Mostar. Many people lived down in cellars. I can remember one particular cellar about 60 feet down, 20 metres down, in darkness with a few guttering candles, people lying around on damp mattresses with a few cans of maybe river water. They would come once a day in the evening to a soup kitchen, and then down into the cellars again. The hospital, well, it was a makeshift hospital because the main hospital was in West Mostar. The makeshift hospital which had been the institute of hygiene, was a charnel house. There were blood-soaked sheets everywhere and patients lying out in the corridors, with the exhausted doctors trying to keep on operating as the injured people came in. I remember one in particular, a young teenaged girl lying naked on a bed, blood-soaked bed, having lost both her legs, at the top of her thighs, as a result of a shell explosion. It was a terrible sight. And in fact, the whole situation in East Mostar at that time was well-reflected in a film, a BBC film, made by a man called Jeremy Bowen at the time that I was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Chamber the comparison between the conditions that you had seen in West Mostar and what you encountered in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was -- the situation between the two, the -- either side of the river, the River Neretva, was totally different. Of course, there had been damage done during the fighting with the Serbs, and the Serbs at this stage were still shelling Mostar and mainly on the east side. But the situation in East Mostar and West Mostar was as different as chalk and cheese, if that will translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm trying to also listen to the French translation and pace myself accordingly. Sir, can you provide any observation to the Chamber in connection with the damage that you saw, and the civilians injured -- that you saw injured or killed? Did this appear to you to be what we might call today collateral damage, or can you tell the Chamber whether you made an assessment or had any assessment that civilian persons and civilian properties were deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was confident myself that this was targeting, a blanket targeting, of the whole of East Mostar, civilians and everyone, to enable the Croats to obtain possession of the whole of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know at that time, and come to know in the months ahead, that that was indeed the HVO objective?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was becoming more and more apparent to me as time -- you know, as the days and the weeks went by, that they had a clear aim of having Mostar as the capital of their so-called Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in passing a man named Slobodan Bozic, and I believe you've said already that he was the Deputy Minister of Defence for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he one of your principal contacts throughout your time in Mostar with ECMM?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, he was one of my principal contacts on the Croat side during that period in Mostar, but he also remained a very close contact for the next five and a half years, but his role over those years changed. He had different roles, but I had constant dealings with him until the time I finally left Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the ABiH side, did you meet and have dealings with an officer named Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the 4th ABiH Corps, which was responsible for that area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in particular Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you share with the Chamber, please, what kind of man he was to deal with, the nature of your relationship with General Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had been a former officer in the JNA, the Yugoslav National Army. He was a professional soldier and I respected him. I had no reason to doubt his integrity or sincerity. He was a man who was determined to fight for the Bosniaks wherever in Bosnia and in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what the situation of the Bosniaks was in East Mostar in terms of their ability, if any, to -- both to either enter the city, if they were outside, or to exit the city?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should start off by saying that although it was the Bosniaks in East Mostar and the Croats in West Mostar, there was an enclave on the west bank, which was a Bosniak enclave, which remained throughout the whole war. So as far as the movement of the Bosniaks or Muslims was concerned, they could not go south because there was the Croat Buna; they could not go east because the Serbs were just four kilometres over the mountains; they could not go west because that was into West Mostar, except into their small enclave; and they couldn't get north because the bridges on the River Neretva were blown, and the only way they could get up to Jablanica was by pack ponies over mountain tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it may have occurred to the Chamber throughout these proceedings, and I want to give you the opportunity to provide an answer if you can. Did you a gain any understanding as to why the Bosniaks, under the terrible conditions that you've indicated this afternoon, why they stayed in East Mostar and did not surrender?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were, first of all, determined not to surrender, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I would like to object to this question. The question as to why somebody else thought or wanted to do something is not within the purview of this witness. I don't think that he would be able to provide us with an answer as to what these people had thought or what they had wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, we understand this witness spent a lot of time in that area. We believe it's quite necessary to us to hear what this witness is going to tell us about the situation at that time. We understand it's just this witness's own recollections. Let me hear what the witness is going to tell us. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, Mr. President. Although -- and although Mostar was very important to the Croats, as I said they wanted it as their capital of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, it was also very important to the Muslims, because this was an original city built during the Ottoman Empire. And in the 1991 census, the proportions were, in Mostar: 35 per cent Muslim; 34 per cent Croat, almost exactly equal; 19 per cent Serb; and the remainder Jews and those who declared themselves on the census as Yugoslavs. Therefore, it had been a totally multi-ethnic city with the highest proportion of mixed marriages in the former Yugoslavia. And the Muslims wanted to ensure that Mostar remained a multi-ethnic city in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges what role, if any, territory played in the war between the Croats and Muslims, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have always believed that the war throughout with the Serbs, Croats, and the Bosniaks was essentially about territory, territory, because they all knew that when the music stopped and negotiations started, possession of territory was 9/10ths of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I also ask you, please, to make any observation you can about the relationship between the military function and the political functions as you saw them at work on all sides, Bosniak and HVO, during the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my view, in Bosnia, and it applied to all sides, the political side and the military side was very closely intertwined. Politicians, political leaders would deal with military matters, and military commanders would deal with political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your involvement there, did you become acquainted to one extent or another, with something called the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Peace Plan was more or less moribund by the time I arrived at the end of June. But I think that one of the reasons why the fighting started between the Croats and the Muslims and the Croats and the Bosniaks was because of a -- perhaps a misunderstanding of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan by the Croats. The plan divided Bosnia into ten provinces, some which had a Croat majority, some which had a Bosniak majority, some which had a Serb majority, but they were not Croat, Muslim, or Serb provinces. In fact, Vance and Owen were particularly careful in not calling them Croat, Muslim, and Serb provinces. They were just given numbers. And the -- but the Croat majority provinces gave the Croats more territory than their numbers actually warranted, so they were very pleased with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and were the first to sign up to it. Now, I think my understanding is that they -- they took these majority provinces as Croat provinces. They were their provinces, and then they started implementing action in the spring in Provinces 8 and 10, which included Mostar, Gornji Vakuf, Vitez, Busovaca, and so on. Tensions rose, and then the first shots were fired in, I think, Busovaca and Gornji Vakuf, and then Mostar exploded on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with what you said just now about the Vance-Owen Plan granting or awarding, if you will, more property -- more territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Bosnian Croats than their percentage of the population, if you recall, can you provide the Chamber with those numbers in terms of what the percentage of the population the Croats represented and what percentage of the territory did they obtain under Vance Owen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gosh, I may not be precise on this, but I think their numbers were about 18 percent in numerical terms. And I think the territory of the provinces gave them close on 25 percent of the land. And of course, I should also add that the -- I said they were not Croat or Muslim provinces. They were intended to be multi-ethnic provinces with the government - the provincial government - based on the ethnic numbers of the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must object once again to this manner of examination. We now have the witness interpreting Vance-Owen's plan. I do not think this is an expert witness, an expert on international law, nor was the witness a party to this plan. Therefore, I do not think that this testimony is relevant, and I do not think it can really help us in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, would you please lead us to the incidents that is more related to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our submission that all of the testimony that we expect of this witness are closely related to the indictment. And I will say in that regard, and just so there is no mystery about it, this witness will only have limited -- important but limited direct dealings with the accused. And to be perfectly candid, that is not the main purpose of his testimony. The main purpose of his testimony is to provide this Chamber with a final overview of the overall events at work in which the crimes alleged occurred and in which these accused conducted themselves. And as you know, the Prosecution is required to prove, one, the existence of international armed conflict, and part of Sir Martin's testimony will relate to that, and we will get to that eventually; about the role of Croatia and the military forces of the Republic of Croatia. We are also required to prove under Article 5 the crimes against humanity charges, that the conduct of the accused took place as part of or in the midst of widespread and systematic conduct of a similar type. This man, who indeed, if not in a technical sense, certainly by his life experience on the ground, is indeed an expert in that sense, not in the sense that someone that the Prosecution has hired or retained to give an opinion. But in a practical, common-sense view, this man has tremendous knowledge of these events. He was a senior official representing the European Union for more than five years on the ground. And we submit, Your Honours, that the testimony that Sir Martin Garrod can provide to this Chamber is extremely important to its overall understanding of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, I understand what you are saying. And we appreciate the testimony by this witness. But in front of us, there are a bundle of documents. I hope your question could be related to all those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They will be, Your Honour. I intend to get to them. And they are clearly in my outline, and I intend to get to them. The nature of the examination, since, Mr. President, you've asked me, is going to be - I propose it to be, and obviously you can give me direction if you choose - to go through a number of these matters to let the witness give Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you his observations and assessments, then to go through some number of the documents, and then proceed with his testimony. That's the way we would intend to proceed. I might say, Mr. President, that I do think the testimony, this testimony, will take sometime, although I can tell you that we are making substantial progress, but I would not want to stand here and tell you, Mr. President, that I thought this witness would be completed in the next hour or two hours. I think his direct examination may take most of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, after hearing Mr. Scott's statement as to the purpose to have this witness testify today, my objection is based on the fact that it's obviously duplicitous of other testimony. He wants to give the Trial Chamber some final, overall view. What I've listened to so far, this Trial Chamber, I believe, has heard evidence from other witnesses saying the exact same things. I would also like to point out that this witness has already testified that he was in Mostar for approximately 90 days or three months, from the very first of July, for a three-month period before he left again to Zenica, and his testimony, in my opinion - and I will raise other objections if need be - is that it is duplicitous, it's not relevant. If he wants to talk about what he observed while he was in Mostar, which he's just testified about, we raise no objection. I concur with the objection of Mr. Par and also raise a further objection based on statement of Mr. Scott that, in fact, this is nothing but duplicitous testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, we understand that this witness is -- this witness is not an expert, but he spent certain time in Mostar at that time, and he has firsthand knowledge of the situation in Mostar at that time. At least he's an independent observer. We would like to hear what this witness is going to tell us on this very subject. But the issue is that we have to go through with all those documents. That's why we intervened, to send a warning to Mr. Scott. Let him be very cautious on this very point. Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I can't scroll back on this screen, and to be quite honest, I can't remember whether there was a pending question or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I help you, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sir Martin was explaining to the Chamber how the intentions of the Vance-Owen Plan were that the provinces were to be multi-ethnic, even though they had majorities of a certain characteristic, and then he was dealing with something to do with provincial governments. So the intention was that each of the divisions which had a majority of either Serbs, Croats or Muslims were still intended to be multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear Judge Clark's recitation of the evidence just --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that, in fact, the nature or thrust of the answer?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in light of counsel's objections, let me ask a couple of other foundation questions. In the course of your mission in Bosnia, not only the time when you were specifically head of CC Mostar, but then also when you were head of RC Zenica, which continued to have Mostar in your jurisdiction, if you will, did you meet with a number of senior Bosnian Croat officials?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met quite a large number of Bosnian Croat officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just name a couple or several to give the Chamber some idea. Did you meet with Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you meet with Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you meet with Dario Kordic in central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you meet with a man named Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You met with the Defence Minister Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, you said, in connection with the Vance-Owen Plan, that the Croats, in your observation, had some misunderstanding about that, and if you've not given a full answer to that at this moment, up to the testimony you've given in the last few minutes, can you please explain to the Chamber what you think that misunderstanding -- or what your assessment of that misunderstanding was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps could I answer -- perhaps I could answer the question by saying the majority -- in fact, nearly all the Croat political leaders that I met, to a greater or lesser extent, sang the same tune, and this was, "We were the first to sign up to the Vance-Owen peace plan. Don't you realise we had 800.000 people in Bosnia before the war, now we've got less than 400.000? Look at those Muslims," they never called them Bosniaks, "The Muslims, they've got all the big cities, Pisevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Travnik, and so on. All we want is Mostar as the capital of our Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." And further - and this was a constant theme - they warned against the establishment of an Islamic fundamentalist state in Bosnia for whom they blamed -- they said that Izetbegovic was planning to do just that. Those were the broad themes which I heard countless times to a greater or lesser extent - indeed, even from the Roman Catholic church, particularly about the Islamic fundamentalism - but this came from all directions. Some, like Jadranko Prlic, were moderate in their language, although they were very tough about perceived antiCroat bias of the west. Others, I say, including the Roman Catholic church, were extremely extreme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, in light of the court's cautions, I'm going to skip over some of your conversation with these officials, but let me direct you to just a couple. You mentioned just now Jadranko Prlic. I'm going to direct your attention to the 2nd of August, 1993. Can you tell the Chamber about a conversation you had with Mr. Prlic around that time and about the freedom of movement or the ability of the Muslims to live wherever they wanted to live or not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I always enjoyed my discussions with Prlic, because I considered him a highly intelligent man and I assumed he was going to be the successor to Mate Boban, but he wasn't. But on that occasion, we were talking about freedom of movement and so on, and he said that -- amongst other things, that people should be free to live where they wanted to live. Well, of course, this was a fine statement, but it didn't help those Bosniaks who were being expelled from West Mostar to East Mostar at that time. They certainly couldn't live where they wanted to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again I'll pick one other conversation. Directing your attention to about the 13th of August, 1993, did you have a meeting or a conversation with a man named Danko Bilnovac? I may have said that wrong, and forgive me if I did.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of police in Siroki Brijeg. And I think -- I think the main point he made - it stuck in my mind at that meeting - was his -- he said that Tito's decision to grant the Muslims the nationality of Muslim by changing the constitution in 1974 had been a great mistake. Because before then, that had been Croats or Serbs who had adopted the Islamic faith, so it was a strong feeling against Tito's decision to establish the nationality of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention, please, to another Bosnian Croat leader, a man named Anto Valenta. Did you have meetings and conversations with Mr. Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a number of meetings with him. He was a vice-president of the HDZ, but his -- he was an intellectual, a thinker, and he had his main -- his main interest was demography. He had written books which he was happy to show anyone. He showed me books on the whole -- how Bosnia should be divided up into three entities which he said was the best solution for the future. And on his map, he had a huge map with the whole of Bosnia with marked -- all the ethnic divisions marked on it down to tiny little pins. And on the pinheads were different colours showing the minute variations of ethnic balance in a particular village. So he was not a very powerful man, certainly when I knew him, but he certainly was a thinker. And as I say, he was the Croats' expert on demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you also have dealings on a number of occasions with this man called Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had regular dealings with Dario Kordic who then was the senior Croat political leader in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, to move us forward as much as possible, with some speed, can you tell us, were his views, as stated to you, and his policies consistent with the ones you've told us about so far this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours, I question and object to the relevancy of what Dario Kordic's views may have been in regards to Mostar -- in regards to Central Bosnia as it relates to Mostar. I think it's irrelevant, and I object on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess that is the background information that this witness is going to tell us. We understand that you have an objection there, which is accurately recorded in the transcript. We'll hear what this witness is going to tell us. When we evaluate this evidence, we will take into consideration your objections on this very point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may answer the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Dario Kordic, although many of our discussions were about immediate problems which were happening at the time, such as the seizure of two BiH helicopters by the HDZ in Medjugorje, the massacre at Stupni Do and so on, but the thrust when we were speaking generally was almost identical to what I've already said was the general theme of the Croat views. And of course, he had very, very close links with Mate Boban, so he was no doubt also reflecting Mate Boban's views.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in summary, and this is my last question on that on this particular group of -- this particular topic, did you find that the political and ethnic views of the Bosnian Croat leadership, for instance, in Central Bosnia was roughly the same or consistent with that which you found in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with exceptions. There were exceptions. And of course, I said some were more extreme than others. If you talked to someone like [Realtime transcript read in error "^"] Kresimir Zubak, one got a very different slant than if one was talking to the real hard-liners. So there were variations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No objection other than line 4 says -- the witness says if you talk to others like -- one got a different slant. I just ask that the witness could please tell that name again so it gets in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name is Kresimir Zubak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, maybe one or two follow-up questions are warranted so it perhaps leaves the Chamber wondering a bit less: When you ended your last question, you said "if one was talking to the real hard-liners". Who were some of the people you would put in that category, the real hard-liners?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the leader for a start, Mate Boban. I mean, he was an extremely hard-liner. There were others whom I got to know when I returned from Zenica to Bosnia -- to Mostar, and I realised -- began to realise who were the hard-liners and who were reasonable people. But I mean, there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object unless we know what the time frame is. This witness just said he realised something after he returned. And I would like to know the time frame for the purposes of either objecting or sitting down in regards to how it relates to the -- this indictment, the time frame of this indictment in this case which we're concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you may ask some questions in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I believe you indicated yesterday, and if I can assist this way, in about mid-October you moved to become the head of RC Zenica and remained in that position until approximately the 18th of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And then I returned to Mostar, I think it was the 19th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know what your ruling is because Mr. Meek so far made objections because that is how we thought to go about the cross-examination. But being the lead counsel, I'd like to make an objection in principle to the cross-examination [as interpreted]. This witness is covering a period of time - and we've finally established it - three months in Mostar in 1993, then return from Zenica, and that happened in April 1994. In April 1994, the Federation was inaugurated by the Washington Accords and the beginning of the political struggle parties and everything else, on the basis of the Washington Accords. These are two completely different settings, especially since the former period was the period of war and covered by the indictment, and the latter period is a period of peace, the establishment of the -- of a state based on the Washington Accords, and these two things do not lend themselves to any comparison. And besides, the latter also falls completely out of the scope of the indictment. I apologise for having taken the floor. And thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you have to understand we already said that we would like to hear some background information of those incidents which happened in Mostar and which is charged in the indictment. We understand there must be a consistent pattern of conduct concerning with the beginning of that incident, the development, and the ending of that kind of incident. We believe that this witness has spent quite a long time in that area, and he is very familiar with the situation during this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So we allow this witness to continue for a while, which means we will take what he said into consideration when we are evaluating the evidence at a later stage. But we also will take in the strong objections raised by the Defence counsel on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I merely wanted to say that the information that this witness has covered principally 1994, 1995, and 1996. And I do not think we should go into that, not only because of the time frame covered by the indictment, and because of the two different political situations in that area. We are having here the period until February 1994 when the witness was not there. The documents speak for themselves with regard to that period. So thank you very much for warning my learned friend that we should move on to documents because that concerns us and the indictment. Things that began to happen after the adoption of the Washington Accords and the establishment of the Federation, especially 1995, 1996, 1997, I think it has nothing to do with this trial because it is not mentioned in the indictment in any manner whatsoever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course, we are not going to 1995 and 1996. But we also understand all those background information is very important for us to understand the international armed conflict, the situations in that area. So, Mr. Scott, would you please proceed in light of the objections raised by Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will continue my examination. And I have to comment for the record -- or note my objection for the record: I appreciate counsel's testimony. I submit to you that the witness's testimony might, in fact, be quite different than what counsel was asserting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention, Sir Martin, specifically to the division of Mostar as you saw it, you've indicated -- can you tell the Chamber again what the Bosnian Croats' view of Mostar was and what role it would play in the Croatian -- first, the community, and then subsequently called the Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Croats were frustrated. As I've said, they constantly said that the Bosniaks, the Muslims, had all the big cities and they had nothing. They just wanted Mostar as the capital of their national identity, cultural identity, religious identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you learn their position or policy towards what role, if any, Muslims would have to play or to exist in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never really discussed. That was never really discussed until later on when we -- you know, a few years later when we started getting down to a unified administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me direct your attention, please. I'll direct the courtroom's attention to Exhibit -- and it will not be in the front of the binder. The exhibits are placed basically numerically, but we will not always follow at the beginning of the book. And this is one instance of that. If I could direct your attention, please, to Exhibit 770.1, 770.1, which is toward the back of the binder. You have that, Sir Martin?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not yet, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The number is in the lower left side, because of some margins on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document, 770.1, is objectionable, and the Defence of Mladen Naletilic objects to this document completely and entirely, based upon the fact that it talks about a time period outside the scope of the indictment, and further, during a time period that this witness was not even in the Mostar area. In all honesty, I'll have to tell the Trial Chamber that there may be in this document some borderline where the time frame of our indictment bleeds over, but much of it is after the time frame of our indictment, so it can't be background, it would be ante-ground -- or post-ground, and it's -- I object, strongly object, to this document, even talking about it, let alone the admission of it, based on it being outside the scope of our indictment that we are concerned with in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, let us hear what this document is about. We understand that this is a kind of report dated 18th April, 1994, and we could read the first paragraph, and we want to know what are the contents in it. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is -- on completing a particular posting, such as head of the Regional Centre Zenica, we were required to make full reports. Sorry. And this is my end-of-tour report, having handed over my post as the head of the Regional Centre Zenica, written -- that was the date I handed it over, on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as stated -- I'm sorry, let me pause. And as stated, this report specifically extends back to the 14th of October, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It goes from the 14th of October, when I took up the appointment, until the 18th of April, when I handed it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note for the record that the indictment itself goes into the first part at least of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention first of all to page 4, specifically item 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. President, on some of these matters, I'll simply give the courtroom a chance to see what's there. Since everyone has the documents in front of them, I will not necessarily take the time to put these on the ELMO, and I suspect that the Chamber does not necessarily want me to read the documents, although in some occasions that might be helpful. But I would proceed, if it pleases the Court, simply by directing the witness to certain passages and then giving everyone a chance to look at that, if that's agreeable, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, have you had a chance to look at paragraph 22 in your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty-two, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that -- is that, in fact, a memorialisation, if you will, of your observations of the policies and views of the Bosnian Croat leadership that you've told us about in the last few minutes this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly -- those were my views at the time and they haven't changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I feel I must note for the record - it's not a complaint but I do want to be clear - given the Court's concern -- some concern about the time taken by this exam, we are having significant lag in the French translation. And it's -- I'm having to wait a considerable amount of time before continuing. And, again, please, I want the translation to understand I'm not complaining, but I'm simply -- in terms of the speed of this examination, it may be substantially slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Sir Martin, I'd like to direct your attention to page 6, and the parts that began under the heading "EU Administration of Mostar." I'm going to ask you some background questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, Mr. President, I'm aware -- I'm well aware of the objections that counsel have stated so far, but I submit, and I ask the Chamber to be allowed -- to allow this witness to at least provide the background for what that was about and how it relates to his observations during this time period, that is during 1993 and early 1994 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I want you to just take a moment -- we are not going to cover this topic at any length. You've heard some of the concerns expressed. Can you simply indicate how did the concept of the EU administration of Mostar come about? And why was it felt that an EU administrator had to be appointed for the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the follow-up to the collapse of the Vance-Owen peace plan and the various negotiations that took place thereafter, the Washington Agreement was signed in March, 1994. This brought about the end of the fighting between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia and the establishment of the Federation between the Croats and the Muslims. Now, because Mostar was the most divided city in the whole of Bosnia, and because it was crucial to the Federation, it was decided - in fact, it was a proposal originally made by David Owen, Lord Owen - that the EU would administer Mostar for a period of two years, to attempt to unify it, to bring in a unified administration, as I say, because it was fundamental to the whole concept of the Federation. And of course, it was also in Mostar where the fighting between the Croats and the Bosniaks had been the fiercest, so the divisions were the deepest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, with that background, please, if I can direct your attention specifically to paragraph 35, if you can take a moment to look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to object to this line of questioning, because we are again proceeding in the same manner. I have understood the points made by the Trial Chamber, and I understand that the Trial Chamber is disposed to let this witness talk about events that are outside the scope of the indictment, and I accept that. But my objection is that if that is allowed, and if this testimony continues along these lines, we will be in a position that we will not know what kind of witness we have in front of us. Is this a witness who will be presenting expert views, although we know that he is not an expert? Or is this a witness who will be presenting his opinions, his thoughts, his observations, regarding certain events? Or is this a witness who is going to be testifying to the facts? In this manner, the Defence finds itself in a position in which we are unable to oppose these views, because if we are told that this is not an expert, we cannot bring in an expert who would counter the views presented by this witness. On the other hand, he is not testifying to the facts, because we -- then we would have a witness saying, "Yes, I saw such and such a thing happen on such and such a day." This is a witness presenting his views. Will this Trial Chamber allow the Defence to bring in a witness who would, in turn, be presenting his own views? So my basic objection is that -- is that we do not want you to allow to bring in a witness whose authority is unassailable and to allow this witness to present his views under the shield of his authority. I do not want to question the credibility or the authority with which this witness speaks, and whether his opinions are founded or not. This is a matter of principle. Do we allow a witness, who is not an expert, to present his opinions? So this would be our basic objection. I have another, very short objection. Now we have documents which reiterate the opinions of the same witness, and this is yet another way in which to put his opinions into the case file. So we are now in a situation where the witness has presented his own opinion, and now we have a document reiterating this opinion, and in the end, the Prosecution will move these documents into evidence, and then we will, in the end, have a situation where the Prosecutor will have both the testimony and the document speaking to the same effect so that will be in a way corroborated, and we object very strongly to this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I concur 100 percent with my learned colleague Mr. Par and would only direct the Trial Chamber's attention to the very first line of paragraph 36 on this Document 770.1, and that says "The EU fact-finding mission completed its visit to Mostar in the last week of March." That's March of 1994. This case, since September the 10th when this trial started, we have been dealing with an indictment and then an amended indictment alleging certain war crimes committed by these accused up through at least January 1994. Why are we dealing with documents that concern a time period two months after the end of whatever allegations have been levelled against my client in this Honourable Tribunal. We are talking now two months after any allegations of war crimes. It's not proper; it's not fair; it's bootlegging this stuff in. And I object strongly on background. And also I agree with everything Mr. Par my colleague said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, I ask to be heard on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You have to be very concise, because it's almost the time for break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Mr. President, these proceedings have gone on for some time. I think the Chamber, by its own observations, knows the Prosecution has not complained about proper cross-examination and proper objections, and it certainly expects the Chamber to make the rulings that both sides will certainly abide by. I object to the series of objections now that have gone on for some minutes. This has risen to the level of obstruction, absolute obstruction. It is full of false statement and characterisation. The testimony of this witness is not outside the scope of the indictment, which was said a few moments ago. It clearly goes to the heart of this indictment, to the period covered in the indictment. Paragraph 26, as one example, says, "... and the conduct continued until at least January 1994." It is not outside the scope of the indictment. They complain first that they don't want to hear the witness's testimony; they just want to see the documents. When we go to the documents, they say they don't want to look at documents; they want to hear from the witness. These series of objections are obstructionist, and I object, Your Honour. I think this witness -- I submit respectfully this witness is important to the Chamber's understanding of this case. Obviously, you will ultimately decide that. But I submit that the Chamber should be given a fair opportunity to receive this witness's evidence, and that is not happening at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We believe that this witness is background and documentary foundation evidence, and he has already given us an independent view and the findings of a very high-ranking independent observer of what happened during that period. And as I pointed out in my remarks just now, the first paragraph of this document says it very clear that "... the appointment which I assumed on 14th October, 1993, relinquished on the 18th April, 1994..." which we believe is covered by the time frame in the indictment. So we are going to hear what this witness is going to tell us on this very subject. And we also remind the Prosecutor about the relations between the testimony and the documents the Prosecutor is going to tender through this witness. We believe that at last, we come back to the document, and we'll concentrate on those documents when we resume. We'll have a break. We'll resume at 4.00. Mr. Usher, would you show the witness out of the room first, please. For the last word, when this Trial Chamber makes a ruling on the subject, the Defence counsel could reserve its view, but we don't want to see any further objections in this direction. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please bring in the witness, Mr. Usher. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I bring up one procedural matter while we wait for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Last week, the Prosecution had delivered to us a motion they had filed for the admission of the statements of two deceased individuals, and I believe the Trial Chamber in the past has entered a ruling that pursuant to the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, that we have 14 days to answer any motion. I want to tell the Court that we -- the Trial Chamber, excuse me, that we intend to file this motion, hopefully tomorrow, if not Wednesday, well within that time period, but I wanted to make sure that we were clear on that 14-day rule. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We believe that this Trial Chamber has already deliberated on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, if I could please direct your attention back to that paragraph 35 of your end-of-tour report marked as Exhibit 770.1, and perhaps the best way to proceed at the moment, before we go on to additional documents, is: When you look at that paragraph, will you simply affirm that that accurately stated your assessment concerning the city of Mostar during the time of your duties as head of RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Chamber, when you -- the views you express in a number of your documents and the reports that you made, were you making those in your role as a senior official of the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, based on my experience and the knowledge that I had gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that the views you state are not simply your personal views, but this represents the assessment at various levels of ECMM as an organisation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Inevitably, there were minor variations of opinion, but I would say that I was reflecting the views of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Sir Martin, in light of some of the objections earlier today: Did you ever find your views or assessments to be substantially out of line with, if I can put it that way, the views of either ECMM people below you or above you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think I can ever recall a significant difference of opinion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And before we leave this document, sir, can I direct you back to page 2, and your paragraph 12? The end of that paragraph starts with the sentence, "In the Mostar region," and I ask you again, was that observation true throughout the time of your association, if you will, with Mostar, even from July of 1993 and continuing to April of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The territory held did not change at all. I put this down to the fact that neither side were prepared, for various reasons, to engage in what we call house-to-house fighting, which is costly in manpower, and therefore nearly all the fighting was done with guns, artillery, mortars, machine-guns and so on. And so no territory, throughout my time in Mostar, changed hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we'll come back to that exhibit in the future as to other topics but in another part of your examination. So let me now turn, again especially in light of the guidance the Chamber has provided, for which I am grateful, if you go back to the beginning of the binder, if you can find your way, please, to Exhibit P359.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, just to set the scene, if you will, of this document, is this a report, in fact, titled "Special Report" dated the 1st of May, 1993, from the head of RC Zenica to the headquarters of the ECMM in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was written by my predecessor as the head of the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention, first of all, to the second full paragraph of that first page. It seems to be marked as number 1, although the format of the document is not always completely clear. But it's the paragraph that has the "1/" in front of it. And again, as I explained earlier, if you'll just look at that paragraph for a moment, I'll ask you a question or two.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did your assessment of the conditions as reflected -- the ones that are addressed in this paragraph, did that assessment continue to be true throughout the time of your involvement both at CC Mostar and at RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In particular, I note the aggressive checkpoints, the restriction of freedom of movement, and harassment of civilians. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a similar way, let me now direct your attention to the next page, toward the middle of the page -- at the end of I guess what would be a full paragraph, the sentence that says "The Muslims are systematically pushed ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first paragraph starts off with "volunteer withdrawal".

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second paragraph starts "last but not least".

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's right above "last but not least".

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, did that continue to be your observation and assessment throughout your tour in ECMM from July through -- July 1993 to April 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, the Croats were still very anxious to achieve their Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber some of the means that the Croats used to accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was -- almost from the time of the start of the fighting, parallel structures emerged. Although both the Croats and the Muslims were fighting the Serbs, they then developed separate armies, separate police forces, separate administrations, separate money. And indeed, they claimed a separate language. So everything, everything was divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can direct your attention to the next paragraph and look at that for a moment, I'll ask you the next question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you explain, please, or give us assistance on the way in which, in your experience, the Vance-Owen plan was used as a "justification" for the seizing of territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croats were delighted with their provinces 8 and 10, which stretched from Mostar all the way up to Vitez, Busovaca and so on. As they clearly considered them to be Croat provinces as opposed to multi-ethnic provinces, it was clear to me what they were attempting to do was to draw a line between cantons -- provinces 8 and 10, and 9, which was the Muslim majority province. And then there was undoubtedly an attempt, such as in Mostar, to make the areas more ethnically clean; in other words, to make it really a Croat province.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I ask you, then, to turn to page 5. There appear to be some handwritten numbers up toward the upper right corner, so if you can make reference to those. If you turn to page 5, the last paragraph beginning on that page, and again I'll ask you just to review that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph which reads -- starts "This analysis ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, and following.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And following. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, Sir Martin, whether the conduct and views expressed here, again, continued to be what you saw and observed and heard from senior Croat officials during your tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had already seen that the Serbs had virtually, by force of arms, achieved their Republika Srpska. And they wanted their own Croat entity, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could then go on to the next exhibit, hopefully this will be a bit easier because we will simply go through the pages. The English documents are followed by a B/C/S translation, so if you'll proceed down, please, through the binder until you get to P373? It would be very close to the -- Mr. Usher, it's this far down the stack. It should be very close to the --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the front?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To the front.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one we've dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P373, marked in the lower, right corner.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we are. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you arrived in Mostar in early July, 1993, and continuing thereafter, were you, at various times, briefed and we might say brought up to speed on the events of the last -- of the previous several weeks and months preceding your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a certain extent, but because we were moving so fast, we were thinking of what was going to happen as opposed to more than what had happened, but of course I had a pretty good idea of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are some references in this document to the HV, on the top of page 4, but I would prefer -- or page 3, I'm sorry, which was a different topic I'd like to come back to in the future. So I think with that, I'm not going to ask Sir Martin to comment further on the document at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to turn down to the next exhibit? It should be just a few pages down, if you follow -- if you pass through the B/C/S translation, there should then be a divider page and then the next exhibit, 386?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just by way of background, turning to the second page of this exhibit, can you just explain to the Chamber, please, who Ole Brix Andersen was and what his position was in ECMM at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The head of the mission would be an EC from the country which at the time held the presidency. At this period, it was Denmark. So in Zagreb, there was the head of the EC Monitor Mission, and his deputy. The deputy was nearly always a political from the political -- from the foreign office, foreign ministry, of the nation concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was he who did the detailed political work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the text of the document that Mr. Brix Andersen's memo seems to be essentially a covering letter for, to the third page of the exhibit, did you come to know, sir, that in the spring, in May of 1993, that a high level ECMM mission had been sent into Bosnia for the purpose of addressing some of the trouble which had started to break out at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Chamber that this is a copy of the report of that fact-finding mission?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And the three individuals concerned would have been the heads of their national delegations of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so if we direct -- if we go to the last page of the English page of this exhibit, the fact-finding mission was headed up by Guy Hart for the British, Pierre Cornee for the French, and Antonio Sanchez for the Spanish delegation? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at paragraph number 3, about the middle of that paragraph, there are references to Mr. Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can just look at that for a moment, please, is that the same Anto Valenta, as far as you know, as the Anto Valenta who you dealt with and you testified about earlier today?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly would have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of the comments, for instance, that are attributed to Mr. Valenta here, do those appear to you to be consistent with the kinds of comments and statements that he made to you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, it was a very stupid response, because there were no Serbs anywhere in the area, and of course, the HVO were a very short distance from Ahmici, which was situated in between Croat Vitez and Croat Vucje Vas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, my objection goes to the non-responsiveness of the answer. The question was very clear, requiring a yes-or-no answer, and I think that this is very non-responsive, and I object to that. He was merely asked did these appear to be consistent comments that this individual may have made to him, and now we've got to a non-responsive answer, and that's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness answered this question with "well, of course." Then he explained his answer, which was clearly stated in that paragraph. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can I then direct your attention to the third page of the report itself, to paragraph numbered 10. Can you please, in looking at that -- can you confirm that that is consistent with what your understanding of what had happened during that time period and the demands and ultimatums that had been made by the Bosnian Croat side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that it would be very much in Mate Boban's character to issue ultimatums. I'm not certain precisely what that letter consisted of, but I'm sure it would have been in connection with taking action on the Vance-Owen plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll say that that letter is in the record, but I won't ask this witness to comment on it further. But it will be available to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next ask you, please, to go to the next page, Item Number 13. Once again, if you'll just focus for a moment on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The sentence at the end of that paragraph which states: "This is not so much as a result of the actions of uncontrolled elements, but rather as a result of the application of deliberate HDZ/HVO policy." Based on your experience and observations, would you share that assessment, and again, throughout the time of your involvement in Bosnia between July 1993 and April 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a close political control of military activities. Both sides often used as an excuse, if some atrocity happened, that there was uncontrolled elements. But I never accepted that because as far as I was concerned, it was the political leaders who made decisions and laid down the policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you could give the Judges some additional assistance as to why you felt that, why you concluded that the statement that these were -- these actions were the result of uncontrolled elements, why you rejected that explanation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to say atrocities or whatever have been conducted by uncontrolled elements is an easy excuse for shedding responsibility. But in my view, it's the political leaders who must take the responsibilities, and then their military commanders under them. And if they make a mistake, they get sacked. But they cannot complain about uncontrolled elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll ask you, then, to go on, please, to Exhibit 386, which again should be the document following the Serbo-Croatian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're absolutely right. 396. If you have that, please, I'll focus your attention -- the only questions I think I will ask you about this will be on paragraphs number 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, to use the words of Mr. Thebault in paragraph number 2, he makes reference to a deliberate policy. And I simply ask you to state to the Chamber your assessment. Did that policy, as described here in connection with freedom of movement, continue to be the practice and policy of the HVO throughout your time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both generally throughout Bosnia and locally in Mostar. And I think maybe by the winter, it was beginning to ease a bit. But I, myself, can remember being blocked for four nights in Gornji Vakuf trying to get down south from Zenica because the HVO had blocked the road. And that was in November. Things gradually eased a little bit towards the winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the effect -- Mr. Thebault uses the terminology here in the first paragraph. He refers to it as "the economic weapon." Can you tell the Chamber your observations: What was the effect of this restriction on movement by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was effect upon food, food convoys. And as far as economy was concerned, for example, from Sarajevo, because the trains were no longer working, any -- and Zenica and so on, any manufacturing, what little manufacturing work that was going on couldn't be brought down south because it was -- the roads were blocked. So it was a complete stifling of the whole system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did that restriction on movement affect the work of the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly had a lot of difficulties, and I gave you a personal example of being blocked for four nights. And it happened to be the coldest week of the whole winter, but that's another matter. But it was a constant problem, and we very often had to use alternative routes. We started discovering that there were alternative routes, narrow little tracks, which we could use. And if necessary, if we were blocked in one direction, sometimes we were able to get round by using another route. But it was a constant problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it may come up in one of the other documents we'll get to in the course of your examination - and at the moment I don't recall for sure, but maybe you can tell us - approximately how long was entry into Mostar blocked from approximately the end of June 1993 until a humanitarian convoy was first allowed in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first convoy -- UNHCR convoy went in, I think it was the end of August. That was -- and from then on, it became not too difficult for UNHCR to get food into Mostar, but there was a long, long period when they just couldn't get in at all. So it was really -- I think the end of August was the first convoy in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll ask you to proceed on, please, to Exhibit 397.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, a number of these things have now become covered in the course of the testimony, but the Court will see that in terms of reference to Mostar being the capital of Herceg-Bosna, et cetera, so I won't go back to those topics at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, let me direct your attention, please, to the second paragraph in what might be described as paragraph numbered 2. There is a 2/ and a paragraph, and then there is another paragraph that appears to start "even if."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could look at that for a moment?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with the two communities -- and I'm specifically addressing your attention to the -- to Mostar, East and West Mostar, from July of 1993 -- actually, according to this document, from May of 1993 to the end of 1993 at least, between the two communities, can you tell the Chamber, please -- give your assessment of who the aggressor was between those two communities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aggression was almost entirely on the Croat side. It was the HVO who was pounding East Mostar into rubble throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That paragraph makes reference to Mr. Thebault's assessment is that it was -- this attack on Mostar was, quote, "planned, precisely organised and conducted." And he says, "Two proofs" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
