utterances.text: I object, Mr. President and Your Honours. This document speaks for itself. The practice of putting the document and then reading directly from it is, I feel, inappropriate. The document speaks for itself. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecutor is asking some questions and asking this witness to verify the facts in those documents, in those statements. We haven't heard the end of the question put forward by the Prosecutor. Let him continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I was laying the foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as a professional military soldier in the Royal Marines for 37 years, when Mr. Thebault makes -- says one of the proofs for concluding this was a planned, precisely organised attack, and he gives his one reason for that, the systematic displacement of more than 1800 Muslims, can you tell us, sir, as a military man, what sort of planning and organisation would be required to coordinate the arrest of 1800 people in a short time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say very considerable planning, and of course, the numbers were very much in excess of 1800 later on, but you cannot just decide, on a moment, to pick up 1800 people and transport them to some form of detention centre. This requires very careful planning and very considerable logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately - and it's just an approximation, sir - in your military experience, how long would it take to plan and organise an operation on that scale?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, it would be weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to object again to the form of these questions. The witness is again placed in a position of an expert - now as a military expert - to provide us with some explanation. We see that this witness had all sorts of qualifications, all sorts of knowledge, that he has a very broad experience, and we are reacting to -- we did not react earlier when the Prosecution asked him, "On the basis of your experience" and so on and so forth, but now, this time, to ask for some expertise, it seems that the Prosecutor is now inducing the witness to testify in a third manner, and I object to further examination in this direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, we don't believe there is any comparison between the two different operations. You may skip that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would submit that the witness has answered the question, and I think it is a fair question and a fair answer to assist this Chamber to make a judgement on what would have been required to organise and carry out that kind of conduct. But I believe that the witness did give his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, Witness, to the -- page 4? There are some page numbers at the top corner of the document, top, right corner of the document, if you could look at page 4? And I just direct your attention to the bottom of that page, the part that's been added by hand, and the statement that, "The planned provinces are not the property of one community or another." Again, is that a reflection of what you saw to be the view of the HVO, again, as you've said this afternoon, and as Mr. Thebault seems to be indicating here, that, for instance, Mostar was a Croat province?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, by now the Vance-Owen Plan was virtually dead, but the principle of having Mostar as their capital remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go, please, to Exhibit 458. And can you just look at that for a moment and I'll ask you a few background questions. The cover memo is again from Mr. Brix Andersen, if you will, not the cover cover, not the fax page, so to speak, but there is a memo dated the 15th of June, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, to orient the Chamber to the next enclosed document, it's titled, "Croat Muslim Relations in Central Bosnia, June, 1993"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just in terms of directing your attention to the first paragraph, can you confirm that this was in fact an ECMM paper prepared for the purpose as stated here of briefing the German government?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, so this is an official assessment of the ECMM prepared specifically for so serious a function as briefing the German government?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct your attention, please, to the paragraph under "Situation," if you can look at that, please. Can you compare, please, or comment whether the statement here about what was happening here in Mostar is consistent with what you saw and observed throughout your time, either directly in Mostar, or as head of RC Zenica. Specifically, paragraph 2 under "Situation."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly how I saw the situation myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to direct your attention down to paragraph -- excuse me, Section Number 3 titled "Summary of Aims," and I want you to look, please, at the HVO aims. Appears to be a., b., c., d..

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say I would agree with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Nothing in your experience, sir, your own personal observations, would be contrary to points a., b., c., and d.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Section Number 5 of the next page, and if you can just read through quickly a., b., c., d., and e.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, which a., b., c., d., and e. Yes, indeed. Yes, I would agree with all those proposals, although the only point I would make is that certainly by the time I returned to Mostar in April 1994, Demirovic had been released from custody, from detention. But I'm not sure when he was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the record, when you refer to Demirovic, this is the person identified in paragraph e. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, as you just indicated, these are -- you said you would agree with all these proposals. Can you tell the Chamber as to these five proposals for action, what if any progress did the HVO make in compliance -- any compliance with these five items by the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of 1993, there was a marginal improvement in a. and b. The HV military activity was still in progress, and there certainly was not unrestricted access to all areas. So I would say marginal improvements by the end of 1993 in a. and b. c. continued, and d. still applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you not -- in the same exhibit, we're not changing exhibits. If you'll page down several pages, it will be the last page in English, there's an enclosed memo titled "From EHRC Zenica" dated the 3rd of June, 1993, subject "HV involvement in BH" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is not so much an objection as an observation. I believe -- and I'd like to ask my colleague, Mr. Scott, we've only been provided with one -- two of three pages, the first and the third, and we don't have page 2. At least it's not in my binder. I don't know about Your Honours' binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We found that document already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you missing page 2 also?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can respond, counsel is absolutely correct. And this is an example of evidence the -- the Prosecution, of course, takes the evidence as it finds it. Counsel is correct. There seems to be two copies of page A1 of 3, no A2, and then A3. And I can simply represent to the Chamber that in my various attempts to find that missing page, I have not been able to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to that last page, right before the -- including --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether we can analyse this document at all if this document is not complete. It is my view that if we are to refer to a document, and if we want to tender a document into evidence, one of the basic prerequisites is for the document to be complete. If this document does not contain all that its original contained, I do not think that we can even take it into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only thing I can say is what I've said already. Obviously if I had that page I would be most happy -- I think the Chamber knows by now I would have provided it. But it's simply the state of the evidence. I can't change that. You'll note that on the fax page at the top of the page, just to indicate that this is consistently what happened, and obviously happened at the time, if you look at the original fax information that some fax machines put on the top of the page, you'll see the fax itself. Starting with the page starting -- "Croat Muslim relations in Central Bosnia", the first page of the report itself. It's fax page 4. Fax page 5. Fax page 6. Fax page 7. Fax page 8. Nothing has been removed. It's just apparently when it was faxed, that's what happened. And I submit, Mr. President, those things happened. Should not be a reason for the Chamber not to receive the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: These things do happen, but in -- not faulting the Prosecutor in this case, it still begs the question that you have a document with one full page missing, and we don't know what the context of that missing page is. And no matter where the fault lies, if it lies nowhere in this courtroom, it's still a basic right of the accused to know the documents and the evidence that are being used against him in this case. We don't know on this document. And I concur on Mr. Par's objection on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand that you have an objection on this very issue. And we'll bear it in mind when we -- when the time comes for us to decide whether to admit those documents into evidence or not. But let the Prosecutor proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I just direct your attention to that last page, and if you could assist us -- perhaps you can; if you cannot assist us, certainly, of course, we'll move on. There is a statement -- you have talked about being -- access and movement of the international organisations being regularly limited or blocked by the HVO. Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall whether one of the areas from which the international organisations were excluded for a long period of time was an area around Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was -- although when this 3rd of June, at this stage, at this stage -- in fact, we did have a team up in Jablanica. But subsequently, we had to withdraw it because the vehicle was hijacked by the mujahedin. But at this stage, we did have a team up in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll simply ask the Chamber to take judicial notice of a calendar. If you work back seven weeks, as stated here, seven weeks from the 3rd of June, that would take you back to the 15th of April, 1993 at which time the blockage of the international organisations around Sovici and Doljani started.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I cannot say -- I'm afraid I just cannot say what the situation was at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Precisely, sir. That's my next question. Were there a number of occasions during your tour when access into certain areas was completely blocked by the HVO? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Absolutely. And some very serious ones, too, including the massacre in Stupni Dol.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can continue on then, please, down to the next exhibit, which I think will be 460, this is a report or document titled "The Way Ahead in Bosnia-Herzegovina" indicating in the upper left corner Ole Brix Andersen, deputy head of mission, 16 June, 1993. If I can direct your attention please, to paragraph number 10 on page 2, and if you'll just look at paragraph 10 and continuing over to the top of the following page, to the end of paragraph 10, can you tell the Judges, please, do you share that assessment, and was that true, during your tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a similar fashion, can I ask you to look for a moment at paragraph number 12? And again I'll simply ask you, based on your experience, your personal observation, were those conditions true, and did they continue to be true, during your time in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention particularly to the second sentence of paragraph 12, is that consistent with what you saw in West Mostar as you told the Chamber several hours ago today?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was clear in my mind that that was the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And with reference to that second -- and forgive me, perhaps I wasn't clear enough. When it says, "In Croat parts of the city, life has returned to normal," is that consistent with what you saw in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Life was pretty normal. There were cafes, shops, and so on, whereas in East Mostar, there was not one single shop of any description whatsoever. Very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph number 18 on the next page, under the section titled "Muslims," I just want to direct your attention to one sentence, reflecting on or connected to something you said earlier today about the amount of property -- or excuse me, territory given to the Bosnian Croats under the Vance-Owen Plan, there is a sentence about halfway down through item 18 which says, "The original map gave areas of Muslim majority, in Jablanica and Konjic, for example, to the Croats." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was that true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, to the best of my knowledge, was true, but I think it was subsequently changed in the revised map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because of the relatively advantageous way -- treatment that the Bosnian Croats received under the Vance-Owen Plan, did you ever hear the initials VOPP interpreted to mean something else?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There certainly was a joke which was that the initials HVO, standing for the Croat Defence Force, stood for "Hvala, Vance-Owen," "Thank you, Vance-Owen," because they were very pleased with the proposals in the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to page 7, I think the last question on this document, page 7, on the upper part of the page, a subparagraph F, this begins to take us a bit into another -- somewhat of a different topic, but I suppose we will just go ahead and cover it now. One of the recommendations being made by ECMM at this time is -- included sanctions, "restrictive measures (sanctions) on the actors in power, (Bosnian Croats as well as Croatians.)" Can you explain to the Chamber why it would be that sanctions would be brought on Croatians or people of the Republic of Croatia and not simply Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- just one minute. This will undoubtedly be because of the Croatian army's involvement in Bosnia, and also because there was an extremely close link between the Croats of Bosnia and the Croatians of Croatia. Indeed, if I could add that the Croats in Bosnia, they all carried Croatian passports. They referred to "our president," meaning President Tudjman. They were able to vote in the Croatian elections and they shared the same national anthem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to send you on, please, to Exhibit P465. And I'm afraid it's going to take a bit more than a moment to -- for to you look at this document, the first page and a half or so, first page and two-thirds, in order to, I think, probably orient yourself sufficiently for me to ask you a couple of questions about it. So if you could just --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Thebault is referring to something -- this something called -- which he refers to in the second paragraph as the Travnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I will note for the Chamber, and for counsel, that this -- a certain additional report goes on, that's actually part of this same document, that's titled on the bottom of the second page, "Travnik Special Report," but again I will not dwell on that particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But are you familiar with what it is that Mr. Thebault is making reference here and making his comments about when he refers to the Travnik case and being a marvellous propaganda operation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was fighting in Travnik in central Bosnia between the Croats and the Bosniaks. A very large number of Croats moved out of Travnik and the surrounding areas, and the question hinged around how much of it was ethnic cleansing by the Bosniaks and how much they had been instructed to leave, even though they may well have been in fear of the mujahedin forces. The -- looking at the following report -- and I have considerable respect for the author or one of the authors of the report whom I know very well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Watkins, Philip Watkins, whose name appears right at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he had been in that area for a long time, then. I would certainly believe what he has said, particularly in his paragraph 5 where he is talking about population moves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'll pause for a moment just so that the Judges can see what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is paragraph 5 of the special report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Let me direct your attention, please, based on that, back to the first page of the exhibit itself, in the lower part of that page, there's a discussion of population or demography, if you will. I want to put this question to you: During your involvement in these issues from approximately early July 1993, at least until April 1994, did you observe that the Croat positions or assessment of the demographics changed in the sense of whether they thought this was to their advantage or disadvantage?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Central Bosnia, it was said to me on a number of occasions by Croats, including men of the church, that they felt deserted by their colleagues down in the south who, they said, were only interested in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and not in them, the Croats in Central Bosnia. If I could go a stage further and say that there was a schism in the high ranks of the HDZ and the Croats. There were some who believed that their whole future lay in concentrating in the south of Bosnia; in other words, in the old Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna stretching from Drvar to Mostar. There were others, including people like Kresimir Zubak and, indeed, people like Ivan Bender and Valentin Zuric who said to me that the future of the Croats lies in Central Bosnia. There was this split. Those who wanted to concentrate in the south. And indeed, another example of that is that -- it's outside the time scale of this trial, but if I might just mention that in 1997, I, with the head of UNHCR in Mostar, had a meeting with the head of the Croat association for displaced people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Defence for Mladen Naletilic certainly, strongly, and vigorously objects to this witness testifying to what happened in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, we are not interested in that case unless you show the relevance to this very case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I can do that, and I think there may be some additional questions to put to the witness. But I think what the witness -- before I put the additional questions, I think, in fairness to the witness, he was citing something as an illustration that illustrated something that was true in 1993 as well. But let me put some additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before you give us this story that you were about to, and depending on whether the Chamber will then allow you to address it or not, perhaps before you get to that point, given these two schools among the Bosnian Croat leadership that you've described, can you explain to the Chamber how it would be to the advantage of one of those groups or the other to consolidate as much Bosnian Croat population, for instance, in Herzegovina at the expense of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I complete answering --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can answer my question first, and then perhaps the Judges will allow you to relate to that -- to illustrate that by your subsequent experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your kind permission, although Mr. Meek is constantly objecting and although you have ruled that only one counsel is allowed to stand up and make objections, but I as the lead counsel need to make a number of objections to the manner in which our witness is questioned today. Mr. President, Your Honours, we cannot allow -- the Defence of Mladen Naletilic cannot allow this questioning to go on in this manner. We're dealing with issues pertaining to Central Bosnia, issues that do not pertain even remotely to my client. We are now talking about some political opinions, observations that have nothing to do with our indictment. We have now gone so far from the original time period; we are now in 1997. Our esteemed witness, for whom we all hold in high esteem, has spoken about many things today; yet, he spoke the least about the period of 1993 and about Mostar and his stay in Mostar. In the period while our esteemed witness was in Zenica, from October to April 1994, we have no reports for that period, yet this witness should confirm the opinions of his predecessors, and we do not know when he was briefed about them and how is then he able to confirm that these opinions that are not his own are true. And also, he speaks about some events in which he never participated. So we strongly object to this line of questioning. And I also thank you for your indulgence for letting me voice my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we already mentioned that we only want to hear the evidence which is related to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which is what you have been hearing, Your Honour, for the vast majority of which -- the witness just now made one reference. He wanted to give an illustration of something from a subsequent time. It is not fair, in my view, respectfully, to say that this witness has been going on and on and on about everything other than 1993. In almost all of this testimony he's talked about 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand that report is dated on the 19th June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we'll allow you to go for a while to see whether there's any relevance to this very case. If not, we have to strike this paragraph out of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I don't know if you recall my last question or not. Let me see if I can phrase it again. Can you explain to the Chamber, based on your observations and your experience in the region, what the advantage would be to one school or the other of the -- what you just described a few moments ago as the Bosnian Croat leadership of moving or consolidating Bosnian Croat population in Herzegovina as opposed to leaving it around Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: For those idealists, shall we call them, who wished to see the Croats remaining in their historical areas of -- in Central Bosnia, there would be a great sadness to vacate Central Bosnia completely, and they would wish to return to those areas where they had large numbers. To others, there are advantages, including military advantages, in consolidating in a smaller area in the south, in other words, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, particularly as that area is entirely contiguous with the mainland of the Republic of Croatia. So there are practical advantages and military advantages to consolidate in the south. But as I say, to others, to people like Zubak, there would be an athema, and he would believe that the future of the Croats would lie in the old lands of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can be allowed to finish this document, please, just one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To conclude on this document, sir, if I could just direct your attention to the second page, not quite halfway down the page, simply there's a paragraph that starts out with the words "it seems Machiavelic, but it is only Balkan." And there are a number of individuals listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, I see you looking a bit perplexed, and if I can assist, if that's not being too presumptuous, on the second page of the -- not the report from Mr. -- not the report from Mr. Watkins, but the second page overall of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at that paragraph for a moment, and it makes reference to individuals. And most of these individuals -- in fact, all of the individuals you've named today, would you agree with Mr. Thebault's assessment that these Bosnian Croat leaders have what you would consider to be extreme views?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would tend to use the word "hard-line." Those were all hard-liners - Boban, Stojic, Kordic and Valenta - absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can see that we are past the time. We can stop there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please show the witness out of the room first? We will resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before the witness is coming, there is a question I would like to ask the Defence counsel. As we all know that the Prosecution's case is approaching its end, so at this moment, would you like to have a Status Conference or some time especially allocated to procedural matters of this case? I would like to hear the initial response from Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall go into all these matters, but not right now, isn't it, once we finished with this witness? Yes, of course, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very briefly, we have agreed a meeting with our friends from the Prosecution, early afternoon tomorrow, and then we shall be -- after that we shall be better prepared for the Status Conference. So with your indulgence, let us talk about it tomorrow or when we finish with this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I'd like to direct your attention now to one more exhibit before we -- we will end with exhibits, at least for a few minutes, and talk about other things, but if I could ask you to look, please, at 532, which should be the next exhibit in the binder? And I apologise that in some of the copies, part of the exhibit number has been cut off at the bottom of the page, but it is a page that up in the upper -- excuse me, it's a document that in the upper left-hand corner bears the date 23 July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've got it, 22 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The actual date of the document is 22 July.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the interests of time, I just want to direct your attention to the first two paragraphs of that document, and I'll ask you a question or two about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, we are getting the French interpretation too strong. Could you please either put the volume down or do something about your headset?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this is dated the 23rd of July, 1993 -- or excuse me, 22nd. Of course, by now you were actually there on the ground yourself, and my question is, again, did the problem with the blockade of roads and this practice or strategy of the HVO, did that continue at least through the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As I mentioned, there was a -- it was definitely slightly easier at the end of the year, but it did continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have, yourself, meetings with senior Bosnian Croat officials to attempt to address this issue of movement, both in terms of the monitoring groups, UNPROFOR, ECMM, but also on behalf of the humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main concern then was movement in and out of Mostar, so I was not -- I wasn't concerning myself directly with movements into central Bosnia. I was more focused on Mostar and the immediate area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, could you please put down the volume of your French channel. It is interfering with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me direct your attention to another topic, and putting aside the documents for a moment, did you have any discussions with General Pasalic of the ABiH about the expulsion of Bosniaks in Mostar during the summer and fall of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used to meet him quite regularly, as I did meet the HVO leadership regularly or the Croat leadership regularly. And I think it was about the 22nd of September that he told me that -- if we're talking about expelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Expulsions.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me then that he was having about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the record, I must enter an objection. The General Pasalic is deceased. There is absolutely no way that we can subpoena him to this Court for any kind of cross-examination or to test the reliability of what this witness is about to say he heard General Pasalic say to him. And that's my objection. He is deceased, and we have no right to confront whatsoever this witness, who will be a witness against my client, should this testimony come into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, we believe that the testimony of this witness on this very issue is relevant to the indictment. And we understand that something happened to one of the persons involved in this conversation. Since this incident is relevant to this issue, we are going to hear what the witness is going to tell us. And of course, we'll not rely entirely on this piece of the evidence, taking into account your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, you may continue to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And General Pasalic told me on that occasion that -- well, between 20 or 90 people being expelled from West Mostar over to the east every night. And indeed, a lot of that, those expulsions, were captured on film in that film that I mentioned earlier on, the Jeremy Bowen film in the BBC series "Assignment". So I don't think there's any doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Sir Martin, that the issue or problem of expulsions continued throughout the time of your association with Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expellings continued until the end of 1996, three and a half years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did they, in fact -- thank you for your answer. But just to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confirm, within the time period you indicated, they did indeed continue until the end of 1993 and the early part of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct your attention, please, to the 15th of August, 1993. Did you have lunch -- attend a luncheon on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was invited by the mayor of Siroki Brijeg - his name was Ivo Culjak - to lunch at his house. It was a fine house, and we had a fine barbecue lunch around his swimming pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you meet anyone in particular that you recall at that luncheon at the mayor of Siroki Brijeg's house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The guest who came and sat down on my right was dressed in camouflage uniform, grey hair, little beard, and introduced himself as "Tuta." He seemed a little bit disappointed when I asked him to repeat his name, assuming that I would know who he was. But at that stage, it did not mean anything to me. We then had an interesting conversation during lunch. He told me that he had been out of Bosnia for 23 years in South America, Germany, Italy, and Holland. He had been running casinos. He told me that his favorite pastimes were poker and backgammon. The subject of our lunch was mainly his concerns and warnings about the establishment of an Islamic fundamentalist state in Bosnia, which he said Izetbegovic was aiming for. I told him that the -- all the Bosnian generals whom I had met in Central Bosnia and raised this specific subject with all insisted, as they downed their glasses of slivovitz, that they certainly did not want to see an Islamic fundamentalist state in Bosnia. But I don't think I convinced Mladen Naletilic on that occasion. I remember remarking at the time, or afterwards, that although Mladen Naletilic certainly had charisma, I would not trust him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn during that conversation that this Tuta had any particular views or attitude toward the man Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I subsequently discovered that he was a great admirer of Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I object to the nonresponsiveness of that answer. He answers it simply "no", and then he went ahead and kept speaking. I ask that it be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I think the Prosecution asked about the contents of the conversation this witness conducted with your client. There's no problem about it. Yes, Mr. Scott. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it makes the record any better, I'll just ask what would have been the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you didn't learn it at that time, did you subsequently learn about any view or attitude that this Tuta had toward Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that he was very close to Mate Boban and a great supporter of him, and he himself confirmed it in an interview which he gave with the "Nacional", Croatian newspaper, in which he expressed his tremendous admiration for Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For the record, could we have a time frame on this supposed interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's a legitimate request.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, can you help us with that, in terms of the particular reference to the article, I think you said in Nacional, approximately when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was -- I remember it well. It was November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever come across a man named Ivan Andabak during your time in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware that Mladen Naletilic was the commander of the so-called Siroki Brijegska Kaznjenicka Bojna, the Siroki Brijeg Convicts Brigade. I was aware that Ivan Andabak was his deputy in that brigade, and I was aware that Vinko Martinovic held a lower position in that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever meet this Mr. Andabak?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the circumstances of meeting Mr. Andabak?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him at a reception in the officers' mess of the Spanish Battalion in Medjugorje. He was a fluent Spanish speaker and had close links with a number of the Spanish officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before moving on, Sir Martin, just so there is no mystery about it, you mentioned you had information about this Vinko Martinovic known as Stela. Is it accurate to say that you did not ever meet this Stela in person?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He asked to come and meet me, but -- I could explain it. But then at the last minute, he didn't appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving on, this has come up to some extent in your prior testimony, but can you explain to the Chamber your observations about the relationship or role in the republic -- of the Republic of Croatia in the events that you saw taking place in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was, of course, extremely close links between the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. As I've already mentioned, they referred to President Tudjman as "our president," and I mentioned the other close connections. But the one other key person was the Defence Minister of Croatia, Gojko Susak, who was actually from Herzegovina, and in fact from Siroki Brijeg. And there were others, Herzegovinians, who were in the government of Croatia, including amongst others, Ivica Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, in your observation, whether the -- some of the people that were in Siroki Brijeg at that time, did they seem to have any -- play any particular role in what was happening, in your experience, in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always felt that Siroki Brijeg, which was a very strong Croat area of Bosnia, some 15 or 20 kilometres west of Mostar, had a strong bearing on what went on in Mostar, because some key people lived there, including Susak, the Croatian Consul General Grubisic, Mladen Naletilic, Vladimir Soljic, Defence Minister and later became Defence Minister and then President of the Federation. So there were a lot of key players living in Siroki Brijeg. So I always felt that that had a strong bearing on what went on in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, my colleague has alerted me that you made reference to the Croatian Consul General, which we didn't seem to pick up in the transcript at this point. Can you repeat that name, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Ciro Grubisic. Shall I correct the spelling of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: C-i-r-o, G-r-u-b-i-s-i-c. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you relate to the Chamber, did you ever observe times when actually someone from the Republic of Croatia, an official from the Republic of Croatia, would lead, if you will, a Bosnian Croat delegation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. In fact, Susak himself led a -- led a Mostar Croat delegation in talks. This was during the time of the EU administration. But he was leading for the Croats and Seljagic was leading for the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was that the only time you recall that happening or did it happen on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For the record, I would request a time frame on this last meeting that the witness spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I trust Mr. Prosecutor will clear it up for us, about that time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reference to Gojko Susak leading the delegation you mentioned a moment ago, can you tell us approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that actually was in January. January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever have conversations within these delegations as to why the Bosnian Croat delegation was led by an official from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, now we are talking about 1996, and it was my understanding from Your Honour's ruling earlier this afternoon that dealing with 1995 and 1996 was not acceptable. And I object on these grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will take your objections into consideration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You can continue, sir, if you remember the question. I'll repeat it from the transcript. Did you ever have conversations within these -- with these delegations as to why the Bosnian Croat delegation was led by an official from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was really because the government of Croatia had such a powerful influence on what was going on with the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina that it was understood that President Tudjman, Susak and others would involve themselves in the matters, Croat matters, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now -- sorry, I'll pause. Now, a moment ago, I asked you if the one instance with Susak was the only occasion. Did you ever -- do you remember an occasion with someone named Mate Granic led a Bosnian Croat delegation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I had quite a lot of dealings with Mate Granic, who was the Foreign Minister of Croatia. The first time I really met him was a meeting we had, I think on the 20th of September, 1993, after an agreement on humanitarian matters between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic. And it was to do -- this particular meeting was to do with the Dretelj detention camp. We met at Grude, and Mate Granic was accompanied by Jadranko Prlic and Vladislav Pogarcic, who was the foreign adviser -- foreign affairs adviser to Mate Boban and also dealt with humanitarian matters. Following the meeting in Grude, we went to the detention camp at Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the purpose of going to Dretelj at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was to do with closing down the Dretelj detention camp. And on arrival, Mate Granic, who is a man for whom I have a lot of respect, spoke to the detainees and told them that they were going to be released, for which he received much applause. A week later, I had confirmation from Vladislav Pogarcic that 500 had been moved from Dretelj to the island of Korcula just off the coast in Croatia. And I received confirmation of that from Claudio Baranzan, the head of the ICRC in Mostar, who confirmed that 500 of been moved temporarily to Korcula before being dispersed, and he -- ICRC was in close touch on all the remaining detainees in Dretelj who were then going to be subsequently released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the island of Korcula --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, we have been asked to slow down. I'll go back to repeat my question. Can you simply tell -- and certainly some people may know. But for the record, can you say to what country does the island of Korcula --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, we didn't get the interpretation this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Diarra, my apology. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, let's go back to the answer you were giving us a moment ago about the visit to Dretelj, if you could just go through that again briefly. You went to Dretelj with people such as Mate Granic. And will you just -- can you take us back through that, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mate Granic, as I say, the foreign minister of the Government of Croatia, was leading the delegation, and he had come down following discussions and an agreement on humanitarian matters between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic. After the meeting in Grude, we all went to the Dretelj detention camp where Mate Granic spoke to the detainees and told them that they were going to be released, for which he received applause. A week later, I heard from Vladislav Pogarcic that 500 had been moved temporarily to the island of Korcula off the Croatian coast, and this was confirmed to me by Claudio Baranzan, the head of the ICRC in Mostar. And he said that the ICRC was monitoring events in Dretelj very closely and was monitoring the release of the remaining detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir Martin, to follow up on that, was there any indication given to you that -- why these 500 detainees were moved to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot answer that. Perhaps there were just not suitable facilities in and around Mostar. I do not know. Maybe the Croatian government was attempting to try and resolve this -- what was by now a political hot potato, the subject of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us about that, how did that subject become a political hot potato?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the fighting in Mostar started, thousands of Muslim men from 16 to 60 were detained and held in camps, the Heliodrom in Mostar, Dretelj, Gabela, Ljubuski, and others. It was exceedingly difficult for us to get inside these detention camps, although we heard warring stories. Only the ICRC were able to gain access, and clearly there was a lot of concern about why these men were being held for all this time and a determination to have them released. Because these were not criminals; they were detained because they were of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did -- if you can take us a step further, then, how did this become a political hot potato?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly because the international community was concerned about these camps. We did not know enough about them. We knew that -- we were concerned whether there was activities going on inside those camps, which would be unacceptable. And in any case, why were they still being held?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you heard of any decision to close any of these camps until the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mate Granic from the Republic of Croatia came to Bosnia and said so?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that was the first indication we had of an intention to start closing the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with these detainees being moved to Korcula, did you have any conversation with this Pogarcic about where they would then go after Korcula?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think as far as I can remember, he said that they would be gradually released, but there was -- I'm afraid I cannot remember. I just cannot remember what he said what would happen to them afterwards. And because I moved up to Zenica, I'm afraid my eye went off that particular problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything -- either that group of detainees or other detainees that were being released would be released as long as they did not return to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard that, but I did not see whether that necessarily could be effected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you state to the Chamber - and again, this has been touched on in the course of the afternoon - but your observations and assessment about the presence and involvement of HV, that is Republic of Croatia armed forces, in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite clear that there was a very considerable Croatian army presence in Bosnia. We had many, many, many reports, and I believed these reports. But then finally, I, myself, on two separate occasions, coming down from Zenica to the south and travelling down the mountain road between Prozor and Tomislavgrad, passed on two separate occasions large Croatian army convoys coming up towards Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when you observed these convoys?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in January and in February 1994. In fact, Prlic subsequently said, "Yes" -- he said, there were HV troops in Bosnia, but he said there were only some 2.600, and these were Croatian army troops who had been born in Bosnia and were returning to fight for their country, volunteers returning to fight for their country. But I'm afraid I took that with a pinch of salt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the numbers involved. And the large number of vehicles and weaponry coming up, these were not volunteers. This was serious military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I need your assistance for a moment. There are two documents that are outside the binder, not in the binder, Mr. President. They are two documents that came up with the Court before, Exhibits IAC-52 and IAC-46. I don't have them. I don't have extra copies here, but if I can ask the registrar's assistance. IAC-46, IAC-52. Mr. President, these were two ECMM documents that some many weeks ago the Chamber indicated that it wanted more information about.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor, what binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They should be in the IAC sets, not the chronological set, but IAC-46 and 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, if I can first ask you to look at, please, IAC-46. And do you recognise -- you recognise this document? I mean, generally by the format and content of the document.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you able to confirm that this is an ECMM report from the headquarters of ECMM to RC Zenica, and then below that the CCs in Bosnia, Tuzla, Mostar and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to propose that this document be placed on the ELMO because we don't have it here with us, and without seeing it, we won't be able to ascertain what it actually is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That document is under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I'd have to check but no, I don't think so. I'm happy to have it shown to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So it could be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just double-check, please. Mr. President, I have no reason to think that either of these documents are under seal. We can put them on the ELMO, I believe. For present purposes, perhaps if the technical booth can just close in as much as possible on the very top, upper left corner, the "from" and "to" information, and the subject and date?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, according to the list that you provided, along with the IAC documents, Exhibit number IAC-46 is under seal, according to this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then I think that's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't have it in my official list, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have reason to think -- not because of the Registry, but I think that information is probably wrong, but we should remove it obviously -- take it from the ELMO quickly. And again, I'm not quarrelling with the Registrar. I think it relates to something -- I have a feeling it relates to something else. But in any event, we won't put it on the ELMO at this time. Perhaps, Mr. Usher - the witness has identified the document; I'm in the Chamber's hands - but perhaps you can just show that copy to Defence counsel and they can look at it in the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While that's taking place, Sir Martin, if you have in front of you there, I think I can say it lying in front of you, IAC-52, can you simply look at that document and just tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's under seal also.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, I won't put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir Martin, I'd just simply again ask you, can you confirm that this is a report from CC Mostar to RC Zenica, a daily summary for the 15th of July, 1993, and being signed by Jesus, acting as head of the CC?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I must have been away at the time. It's a daily report sent by my deputy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Usher, if you could please again show IAC-52 to counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Judge Diarra is not aware that there is a French translation at the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Judge Clark, for assisting on that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. President, I'm going to let the documents speak for themselves but again because of the inquiries the Chamber made previously, I was just asking this witness to identify them further for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we leave this topic, Sir Martin, if I could ask you to go in the binder back again to your end-of-tour report, which is Exhibit 770.1? Again, it's getting more toward the back of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've located it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can direct your particular attention in this regard to your paragraphs 14 and 15, starting on the bottom of page 2 of your end-of-tour report, and when you've had a moment to look at that, I'll just have a question or two for you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do those two paragraphs essentially serve as a summary of your assessment and observations about the HV involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina in that approximate six-month period from October, 1993 to April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in particular, I was never able to establish whether this large movement of HV forces was offensive or defensive. They were heading up towards Prozor. If the Croats had lost Prozor, the Bosniaks would have been down to Mostar, and so Prozor was absolutely crucial. But it could have been offensive, as I've indicated in paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the end of paragraph 15 on page 3 of your report, is it correct that you and your teams also had observed a, quote, "Build-up of HVO/HV in the Buna area south of Mostar"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I think that takes us then back to a final set of documents that I'd like to take you through, starting with Exhibit 553.1 in your binder. Approximately -- very roughly about in the middle of the binder, if that helps at all. I think, sir, in watching you, I think it's going to be further -- not back that way but further the other way.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Right about perhaps where you are, somewhere in that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 553.1. It is a daily summary for the 1st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is looking for that document, 553.1, I believe that Mr. Scott, my friend from the Prosecution side, had asked a question -- the last question was whether this witness or his teams had "observed" a build-up in the area of Mostar as based on the previous document. The record ought to reflect that the previous document did not say "observed" whatsoever, but only said "aware of". And there's a big difference between observation and being aware by some third or fourth sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, would you please make it clear for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I accept that that is a difference, and I appreciate what counsel has said. Perhaps I can come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you found that document?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found 553.1, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we will come back to that document, if the Court will allow, rather than lose our place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, 553.1, simply, sir, can you confirm that this is a daily summary that is, in fact, over your name or signature?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the reference under Item 3 about the middle of the page approximately, is this a reference, to your knowledge, of the Colonel Andabak that you've mentioned earlier today as someone you knew to be associated with the HVO special forces?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but the spelling is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how do you understand it should be corrected?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be A-N-D-A-B-A-K.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just in reference, the things you've told us about in the course of your testimony at the bottom of that page, you make a reference, in fact, to a scheduled meeting with Mr. Prlic, the president of the HVO, on the 2nd of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can go, then, to Exhibit 555.2. Simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, a number of these documents are now simply going to be, to some extent, memorialised or a record some of the items that the witness has told us about. And I'll just take him through, to some extent, his own records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On 555.2, you've told us, sir, on several occasions about a meeting with this Mr. Prlic. And if I direct your attention to paragraph 2, and carrying over to the second page, just look at that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does this report memorialise, to some extent at least, the conversation that you told us about earlier today with Mr. Prlic where he said something to the effect that people should be allowed to live wherever they want to live, but it appeared to you the reality on the ground was something different?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Of course, it was much longer than that. This is just a very short summary of what was said, But that is essentially the point he was making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We can go on, please, then to Exhibit 559. Is this a report from HRC Zenica to the headquarters of ECMM dated 4th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that I will skip over the first part of the document; let it speak for itself. If I can direct your attention to paragraph number 2 on the middle of the second page, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could once again just scan down that next couple of paragraphs about the situation in Mostar, I'll have a question or two for you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again I'll just simply ask you, sir, especially given the hour, can you confirm that, in fact, those observations were consistent with your own and was an accurate assessment of the conditions in Mostar that you saw throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a good and fair assessment indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention down to subitem B, as in "boy", does that make a reference to the various mass arrests or at least some of the mass arrests that you had made reference to earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look over on the next page, skipping down to the first -- well, it's hard -- skipping down to the paragraph that starts with "Hints".

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist the Chamber in any way with any discussions or proposals that were put forward by the HVO around August of 1993 about something called a transit camp?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of it, but I'm afraid I just cannot remember the details of this transit camp in Ljubuski. I regret I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about -- in the next paragraph -- about, again, putting approximately 1.000 Muslim males on another Croatia island called Obenjan [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have got a vague recollection but not a precise recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can assist. I don't want you -- Sir, no one in the courtroom I'm sure wants you to guess, but if you can assist us, can you please do so. Any other information you can provide in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm very sorry. I'm afraid I really don't think I can produce anything concrete on this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. All right. I think we can move on, then, to Exhibit 559. Is this a report from CC Mostar to RC Zenica, a daily summary of 7 August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got one, 561. 559, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I made a mistake, I apologise. You're absolutely right. My apology. 561.1.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to confirm, if you can, please, is that a report from CC Mostar to RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, direct your attention, well, to the last page for a moment just to further orient you, was this a report that went out over your name or at least your signature --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- well, your signature or your name?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention back to paragraph number 3 --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- can you recall anything more -- can you add anything more that you recall about this person called Juka?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Juka was someone who was not known to me. I'd heard the name but I did not know anything about him. And then, of course, when I left for central Bosnia, when I returned, his name was never ever mentioned again. So I did not know -- I'd heard the name, I'd heard that he was a leader, but I did not know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And going, moving up to paragraph number 2, just simply makes a reference to the "BIH war president in Jablanica welcoming ECMM presence back in Jablanica." Now, when you say the "BIH war president," would that be for - perhaps, again, it's obvious, but for the record we can't assume - is that for the HVO side or the Bosniak side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Bosniak side, the Bosniak side in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you help the Chamber with any distinction you saw between the Bosniak side wanting the presence of the ECMM and granting access to areas under their control in contrast to the policy of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jablanica was an interesting case in point. This was a Bosniak town which the Croats very much wanted to seize, because -- largely because of the hydroelectric power plants. We had a -- and there were small pockets of Croats up around the Konjic area. So they were -- both sides were interested in the Jablanica, Konjic area. We had one of our teams, as I mentioned yesterday, up in Jablanica. It was based in Jablanica. But right at the end of June, they were hijacked by the mujahedin and their very expensive Mercedes four-while-drive car was stolen. Therefore the team had to come out because they had no transport. It took us some two or three months to get a team established back in Jablanica again. The Bosniaks -- clearly from here -- Cibo wanted us back in Jablanica, and funnily enough, the Croats, for their own reasons, said they would welcome a presence. In fact, people like Prlic and so on said they would like us to get back to Jablanica so that our teams could report on the condition of the Croats in the Konjic area. So there were mixed -- mixed emotions about us returning, getting back into Jablanica. I hope that's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think perhaps in part. When you say "mixed feelings" just now, mixed feelings on whose part? On ECMM's part or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. We were very anxious -- we were very anxious to get back into Jablanica because it was a big gap in our knowledge, information. We had no information coming in from that area at all, and it was a key, key area. But when I say "mixed feelings," it was unusual for both the Bosniaks and the Croats, for different reasons, to be quite keen that we were back in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, before leaving this document, if I can ask you to look at the last entry under item 9, you mentioned, sir, much earlier today, that one of the persons you dealt with frequently was Mr. Bozic, the Deputy Minister of Defence. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say, "Pursue entry into Mostar." So can we take it from that, sir, that as of the date of this document, the 7th of August, 1993, Mostar was still blocked to --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they must have been because I'm using the words "pursue entry," and I was doing that on an almost daily basis, trying to convince Slobodan Bozic and others that it was in everyone's interest for us to get back in as soon as possible. So on this date, we clearly had not been able to get back into Mostar yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, then, to go, please, to Exhibit 565.2?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm, please, this is a copy of a daily summary for the 15th of August, 1993, over your name, to RC Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at the content of this document starting on the lower part of the first page and continuing on over to the second page, can you confirm to the Chamber, sir, that this was a report in part that discusses your lunch meeting with Tuta?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the top of the second page, there is a reference to some comment about "though he was currently serving in Gornji Vakuf." Was that based on something that Tuta told you at the time -- during the luncheon?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been, it must have been, because I had no knowledge of Mladen Naletilic before that meeting, and so it must have been he who told me that he was currently based in Gornji Vakuf and complained that the British had fired on him. So it could only have come from him because I certainly didn't get the information from anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph, does that memorialise, at least, again, in part, the conversation you told us about earlier today with Mr. Tuta concerning his views about the Islamic fundamentalist state?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it accurate to say he was reflected here that in the course of your conversations here with Mr. Tuta during that lunch that he made analogies or references to -- analogies of gambling to the conduct of warfare?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that will have been correct because I will have written this within an hour or two. I would have probably written this as soon as I got back from that lunch, so it would have been very fresh in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again directing your attention to item 9, you say that again on the 15th of August, 1993, "Attempt once more to enter Mostar"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it must have been just about this time that we succeeded in getting in, but I can't guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can next ask to you look at Exhibit 600? And the only thing I'm going to ask you to do, sir, on that one, is, again, can you confirm that that is a monitor report, in fact, from one of the Mostar teams, M-2, to the regional -- I'm sorry, not to the regional centre initially but to the coordination centre in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN GARROD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, one Spanish and one Dutch monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to suggest, if we can, that this might be a good place to stop. I can tell the Chamber that I'm very close to, I think, concluding. I think I have approximately, looking at my outline, about four more documents to put to the witness, none of which should take, I think, a long amount of time, so we should be able to finish in the first two minutes tomorrow -- well, I was going to say morning but tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will stop here. Mr. Usher, would you please show the witness out of the room? Tomorrow morning, this courtroom will be used for another case, so I advise all of you to take all your documents out of this courtroom. We will resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.
